title: Impact of Monetary Authority of Singapore's $7.4 Billion Loss on Government Budget
what_it_is: Impact of Monetary Authority of Singapore's $7.4 Billion Loss on Government Budget

sections.label: Net loss currency translation effect
sections.summary: The $7.4 billion net loss reflected translating the foreign currency value of the Official Foreign Reserves into Singapore dollars.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The net loss of $7.4 billion reflected a currency translation effect, in other words the effect of translating the foreign currency value of the Official Foreign Reserves (OFR) into Singapore dollars.

sections.label: MAS FY2021/2022 investment gains
sections.summary: MAS made $4 billion investment gains on the OFR, outweighed by $8.7 billion negative currency translation effects from a stronger Singapore dollar.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: For FY2021/2022, MAS made investment gains of $4 billion on the OFR.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: These investment gains were, however, outweighed by the negative currency translation effects of $8.7 billion arising from a stronger Singapore dollar.

sections.label: Net loss and NIR
sections.summary: MAS' reported net loss in the last financial year has no impact on the NIR available to the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: MAS’ reported net loss in the last FY has no impact on the NIR that is available to the Government.

sections.label: Smoothened MAS contributions to Government
sections.summary: Since FY2019 the Government required MAS contributions paid in equal proportions over three years, so it will receive $1.1 billion despite MAS' FY2021/2022 net loss.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: This is why, since FY2019, the Government has smoothened the revenue volatility by requiring the annual contributions made by MAS to be paid in equal proportions over a period of three years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: This means that even though MAS recorded a net loss for FY2021/2022, the Government will receive $1.1 billion from MAS, based on the contributions accrued for the previous two financial years, when MAS recorded net profits.

sections.label: MAS contribution formula and smoothening
sections.summary: MAS contributions are in lieu of corporate income tax, based on 17% of net profit after offsetting cumulative losses, with a FY2019 smoothening formula over three years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: I have explained just now that MAS' contributions are in lieu of corporate income tax and there is formula for it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: It is based on 17% of the net profit for the year, after offsetting cumulative losses from previous years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On top of that annual contribution, in FY2019, we also introduced a smoothening formula so that the contributions made by MAS are paid in equal proportions over a period of three years.

sections.label: MAS expenses and investment income
sections.summary: MAS may spend more when borrowing for money market operations, but rising interest rates will help raise investment income from foreign asset holdings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On the expense side, MAS will have to spend more, perhaps, when it needs to borrow as part of money market operations to manage banking system liquidity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But on the investment side, over the medium term, rising interest rates will also help to raise investment income from our foreign asset holdings.

sections.label: NIRC and long-term returns
sections.summary: The NIRC in the Budget is based on the long-term expected real rate of return applied to the net asset base of MAS, GIC and Temasek, not short-term performance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In the end, regarding these performances, it is not so much whether they do well, or not so well on an annual basis, because what matters to us is the NIRC that comes into the Budget.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: And as we have explained time and again, that is not based on short-term investment performance, which can be up or down, depending on market volatility, but it is on the long-term expected real rate of return, which is determined and then applied, as I have mentioned just now, on the net asset base of MAS, GIC and Temasek respectively for us to work out the NIRC into the Budget.
